result.process_description:
Title: Service for Your Fridge

Your fridge produces strange noises.
You describe the symptoms, and send them together with the type of fridge to the central fridge service center.
They select a local service facility (which all have their own way of interacting with customers).
The service facility makes an appointment.
They arrive at a random time, and sometimes have to leave without repairing your fridge, because they need additional parts.
After your fridge is repaired, you have to confirm that it is OK again.
You can rate the service facility.

result.rule: Several unconditional outgoing flows from one activity can all proceed. Use a gateway when the description requires a decision or synchronization.
Allow multiple start or end events when the description has distinct triggers or outcomes. Do not force all outcomes into one end.
Do not create separate pools for ordinary internal roles unless the description treats them as independent communicating participants.
Do not merge separately described actions into one task or split one stated action without a process reason. Preserve described dependencies.
Do not infer a task subtype only from a verb in its label; require supporting meaning in the full description.
An ordinary embedded subprocess participates in normal sequence flow and may contain its own starts, ends, activities, gateways and flows.

result.rule: When the description says that a party outside the process produces items that the process receives (for example, writes or sends several updates or offers about the student), at times the description does not specify, and the description gives no activities of that party other than producing those items: Model each such receipt as a message intermediate catch event, or as a receive task, that waits for the item. Label it with the receiving verb and object the description uses for it, and do not label it with a send or write verb that describes the outside party's production. Keep send and write tasks for work the modeled process itself performs. Use one catch event per awaited item when the description states a count.

When the description says an external party, such as the customer, chooses among several options (for example, a set of alternatives or quantities) before the company starts production, and the choices determine what later teams build: Model each such choice as its own step performed by that external party: a user task placed in a separate participant or lane for that party, with one task per decision the description names, sequenced before the production activities that depend on it. Do not fold the choices into a single generic input or into the company's own work step.

When the description attributes its own processing steps to an outside party (such as staged computation, sending a reply, or reporting a delay) that happen between the process's request and a reply the process waits for: Model each processing step the description attributes to that outside party as a task inside a separate participant pool for that party, in the order the description gives. Connect the process's request to that pool with a message flow. Connect the party's messages back to the process with message flows into message intermediate catch events or receive tasks. Do not omit the party's steps, and do not reduce them to bare waits in the process pool.

When the description says that a request is sent to a party outside the process and replies from that party are awaited, but the description does not describe any activities or decisions of that party: Model the request as a send task in the participant's own process and model each awaited reply as a message intermediate catch event that follows it, all within the same participant process. Do not add a separate pool for that party, and do not add message flows from the send task to it or from it to the catch events.
